summary: Block-based (Blockly) logic: blocks compile to JavaScript that runs when a signal fires and writes the node's output ports.
description: Logic Builder stores a visual block program (Google Blockly) in its `workspace` parameter; the editor generates plain JavaScript from the blocks into the hidden `generatedCode` parameter, and the runtime compiles and executes that code. Execution is strictly signal-driven: the logic runs when the `run` signal input (or a block-defined signal input) fires — changing an input value alone never executes it. The generated code runs with `Inputs`, `Outputs`, `Noodl`, `Variables`, `Objects`, `Arrays` and `sendSignalOnOutput` in scope, so blocks can read and write global Noodl Variables/Objects/Arrays. Every `Outputs["name"] = ...` in the program becomes a value output that updates after each run; a runtime exception lands in the `error` string output.
whenToUse: Reach for it when logic must be authorable without writing JavaScript. For anything beyond what the block set expresses — async work, loops over API data, library calls — use JavaScriptFunction (Function); for a one-line computation use Expression.

ports.run: Signal input (connections only, hidden in the property panel); fires one execution of the block program.
ports.workspace: Edit-only Blockly workspace JSON, authored in the block editor — not written by hand.
ports.generatedCode: Edit-only JavaScript the editor generates from the blocks; the runtime executes exactly this text.
ports.error: String value output holding the message of the last execution error, empty when the last run succeeded.

runtimeBehavior: Ports are runtime-determined from the generated code: the editor scans `generatedCode` for `Outputs["name"]` assignments and publishes a value output per name (it publishes ports only when at least one output is detected). Input, signal-input and signal-output detection is not currently implemented in the editor's port scan, so data must reach the program through Noodl Variables/Objects rather than input connections; the runtime would register input ports on demand, but the editor does not surface them. An authoring tool should treat `workspace`/`generatedCode` as editor-managed, wire signals to `run`, and read only outputs that appear as `Outputs["..."]` in the generated code.
patterns: Button `onClick` → `run`, with an `Outputs["..."]` value wired to a Text — the minimal block-program shape.
Blocks read and write `Noodl.Variables` to exchange state with the rest of the app instead of using input ports.
antiPatterns: Expecting the logic to re-run when connected values change — nothing executes until a signal fires.
Hand-editing `generatedCode`; the block editor overwrites it from `workspace`.
